conflicts.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council August 27, 2020 (w/ captions)
conflicts.issue: Transparency, Agenda Notice, and County Responsibility for $338,000 Learning Centers Funding
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-1 on approving $338,000 from the City's $5 million COVID Relief Fund for community learning centers, contrasting urgent pandemic student need against lack of work-session agenda transparency and Durham County's primary statutory role in funding public education.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve $338,000 in emergency COVID Relief funds immediately to launch 11 weeks of learning center seats by September 8 while emphasizing future funding must come from Durham County, DPS, and private donors.
side_a_arguments: Providing 11 weeks of learning center support for 338 students addresses an acute pandemic need before the September 8 start date.
The DPS Foundation is actively fundraising for the second semester, and partial immediate support is better than leaving students unserved.
conflicts.side_b_position: Withhold support because the funding request bypassed normal work-session public agenda notice and disproportionately taps the City's limited $5 million COVID Relief Fund.
side_b_arguments: The original ask and supporting documents never appeared on the work session agenda and were only placed on a late special-meeting agenda.
Durham County received far greater federal CARES funding and carries legal responsibility for funding Durham Public Schools.
conflicts.resolution: Motion passed 5-1 on roll call (Schewel, Johnson, Caballero, Middleton, Reece Aye; Freeman Nay).

conflicts.issue: UDO Amendment / Residential Development Case (Mr. Sivers) and Stormwater Flooding Concerns

conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the consistency statement and UDO amendment based on post-Planning Commission changes and promised housing price points.
side_a_arguments: Developer made revisions following the Planning Commission hearing.
Project delivers housing at the target price point committed by the applicant.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the UDO amendment and consistency statement amid recurring neighborhood flooding concerns.
side_b_arguments: Council Member DeDreana Freeman warned that heavy downpour flooding repeatedly affects residents across different parts of the city and is not adequately on Council's radar.
conflicts.resolution: Both the consistency statement and UDO ordinance passed 4-2.

Community Development monitors affordability compliance for affordable units.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council August 24, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Structure of Ward 3 Finalist Interviews (Time Limits, Advance Questions, and Finalist Count)
conflicts.summary: Council members held differing views on shortening questioning rounds from eight to five minutes, requiring or encouraging advance submission of questions, permitting PowerPoint slides, and whether to interview four instead of five finalists.
conflicts.side_a_position: Favor shorter five-minute rounds, advance question sharing with candidates and colleagues, or reducing to four finalists to keep the August 27 interview meeting concise.
side_a_arguments: Five 50-minute Zoom interviews create an exhausting four-hour session.
Sharing questions ahead of time avoids duplicate questioning and helps candidates prepare concise responses.
Limiting the pool to four finalists could also shorten the meeting if time is a major concern.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain the established eight-minute questioning cap and preserve unscripted live questioning (or require PowerPoints if time is cut).
side_b_arguments: Council is a deliberative body that needs to see candidates think and engage on their feet rather than read scripted answers.
Individual members can already govern themselves and use fewer than eight minutes without lowering the formal cap.
Cutting questioning to five minutes without a PowerPoint option could limit the information gathered from candidates.
conflicts.resolution: Council maintained five finalists, kept the eight-minute cap (with Charlie Reece voluntarily taking five minutes), allowed optional advance sharing of questions and candidate materials, and prohibited PowerPoints in three-minute openings.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council June 10, 2020 (with captions)
conflicts.issue: Neighborhood Protection Overlay (NPO) UDO Initiation Revisions
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-1 (with Caballero absent) on requiring governing-body initiation before staff processes NPO requests.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the NPO text amendment to clarify expectations, conserve limited staff bandwidth, and prevent exclusionary neighborhood overlays.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Schewel cited proliferation of NPOs in Raleigh and Chapel Hill used to block housing diversity in privileged neighborhoods.
Staff noted the Old West Durham NPO experienced a four-year wait and heavy volunteer burden without early Council guidance.
Council Members Charlie Reece and Mark-Anthony Middleton supported the text amendment as clarifying the process.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the NPO text amendment as weakening citizen-led neighborhood protections.
side_b_arguments: Resident speaker Ms. Plass argued early Council gatekeeping politicizes NPOs before rules are formed and creates an unequal standard compared to developers.
Council Member DeDreana Freeman cast the lone Nay vote on both motions.
conflicts.resolution: Both the consistency statement and ordinance passed 4-1 with Caballero absent/non-voting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Durham City Council Meeting May 27, 2020 (with closed captions)
conflicts.issue: Racial Equity in Budget Reductions and New Transportation Financial Manager Position
conflicts.summary: Council members debated whether COVID-19 budget adjustments adequately centered racial equity and flagged the proposed Transportation Financial Manager position for further review against competing city priorities.
conflicts.side_a_position: Insist on deeper racial equity safeguards in cost-cutting and scrutinize adding a new Transportation Financial Manager position relative to other city needs.
side_a_arguments: DeDreana Freeman stated the council must avoid rushing into easy cost cuts with inequitable outcomes ('I can't do a Katrina outcome').
Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson asked to flag the new Transportation Financial Manager position to weigh against all other potential city needs.
conflicts.side_b_position: Highlight equitable transit spending and potential Transit-fund or CARES Act offsets for the Transportation position.
side_b_arguments: Transportation staff noted GoDurham transit expansion is the largest budget increase and serves a ridership roughly 90% people of color, and City Manager Tom Bonfield stated service restoration applies an equity lens.
Charlie Reece pointed out Transportation Director Sean proposed shifting the position from the General Fund to Transit, and Javiera Caballero asked whether CARES Act funds could help.
conflicts.resolution: Staff recorded the Transportation Financial Manager position and Parks and Recreation staffing breakdown as flagged follow-up items with no formal vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session July 23, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Gun Violence Response Priorities (ShotSpotter and Violence Interrupters) vs. Participatory Budgeting Equity Scrutiny
conflicts.summary: During a wide-ranging work session debate following recent fatal gun violence, council members clashed over prioritizing urgent gun-violence interventions such as ShotSpotter and violence interrupters versus repeated critiques of Participatory Budgeting's equity outcomes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize immediate action and funding for gun-violence interventions—including violence interrupters and testing ShotSpotter—while subjecting all city initiatives, including Participatory Budgeting, to equal equity scrutiny.
side_a_arguments: Addressing gun violence affecting Durham children is far more urgent than Participatory Budgeting.
Children's lives justify experimenting with tools like ShotSpotter, and Council can discontinue it if evidence proves it ineffective.
Council must schedule concrete funding and operational steps for violence interrupters and gun-violence prevention.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid conflating the gun-violence crisis with Participatory Budgeting criticism, correct incomplete PB demographic data claims, and schedule a dedicated PB staff and NCCU evaluation briefing alongside advancing the Community Safety Task Force and violence interrupters.
side_b_arguments: Claims that Participatory Budgeting failed its equity goals rely on incomplete demographic data because paper ballots and DPS student votes lacked racial data.
PB staff, the steering committee, and North Carolina Central University produced a full evaluation with improvement proposals that merit an accurate agenda briefing.
Crisis response and expanding violence interrupters should move forward in concert with the Community Safety & Wellness Task Force.
conflicts.resolution: Informational discussion; Mayor Steve Schewel agreed to work with the City Manager to schedule future work-session discussions on both gun-violence/violence-interrupter funding and the Participatory Budgeting evaluation.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Durham City Council Meeting May 28, 2020 (with captions)
conflicts.issue: Form and Financial Specificity of City Council Outreach to Durham County on Homeowner Tax Relief
conflicts.summary: While all council members favored partnering with Durham County on an expanded long-term low-income homeowner tax relief program, members differed on whether to send a letter citing roughly $1 million, send a letter without a specific dollar figure, or adopt a formally voted City Council statement.
conflicts.side_a_position: Send a Council-signed letter committing roughly $1 million in city funds (or a formal letter without a dollar figure) to invite a County proposal.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece suggested a joint letter under all members' signatures indicating readiness to commit around $1 million in administration and grants.
Mayor Steve Schewel supported a Council letter inviting a County proposal at any time during the fiscal year without naming a specific dollar figure because Council lacked consensus on a number.
conflicts.side_b_position: Issue an official voted City Council statement carrying the full formal weight of the governing body rather than an informal letter.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton argued the issue crossed the letter-writing threshold and needed a formal voted Council statement with the clerk's stamp and raised seal to signal Durham's commitment.
conflicts.resolution: Council suspended the rules 6-0 and unanimously passed Middleton's motion (seconded by DeDreana Freeman) 6-0 to adopt an official City Council statement without a fixed dollar amount.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session May 21, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Vendor Sourcing and Equity Conditions for Cover Durham Mask Project
conflicts.summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman questioned sourcing all 50,000 masks from Original Mattress Factory in Raleigh rather than local Durham or POC-owned producers, while Mayor Steve Schewel and Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson noted the direct vendor allocation was already set and added hiring and transit-rider amendments instead.
conflicts.side_a_position: Direct mask procurement funding to local Durham or people-of-color-owned businesses rather than an out-of-county vendor in Raleigh.
side_a_arguments: DeDreana Freeman noted local producers such as LCI were already making masks in Durham and urged finding ways to fund local or POC-owned businesses.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve the transfer as structured for Original Mattress Factory while requesting prioritization of transit riders and hiring people of color for distribution.
side_b_arguments: Jillian Johnson noted the funding was already designated to go directly to Original Mattress Factory so a POC-owned manufacturer could not be substituted at this stage.
Requesting the nonprofit prioritize hiring people of color in distribution and prioritizing GoDurham transit riders addressed equity goals.
conflicts.resolution: Jillian Johnson's motion incorporating both friendly amendments (seconded by Mark-Anthony Middleton) passed 6-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session May 21, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Small Business COVID-19 Relief Fund Timeline, Sizing, and Equity Design
conflicts.summary: Council members sharply criticized OEWD's presentation for omitting a concrete fund size, delaying check writing until July 1 while searching for a CDFI partner, and relying on traditional underwriting criteria that could preserve racial disparities.
conflicts.side_a_position: Commit funding immediately, deploy already-budgeted Built to Last funds by early June, and redesign eligibility around racial equity rather than waiting for July 1.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton objected that the plan omitted a fund size, lagged behind peer NC cities, and came without a ready 'yea or nay' structure.
Jillian Johnson urged immediately deploying the $300,000 already budgeted for Built to Last rather than waiting for the new fiscal year.
DeDreana Freeman warned that relying on existing credit and longevity criteria keeps racial disparities intact and urged equitable relief for struggling cash-flowing businesses.
conflicts.side_b_position: Work with Council, the City Manager, Duke University's $1 million commitment, and a vetted CDFI partner to bring a structured budget and program to the next council meeting for July 1 disbursement.
side_b_arguments: OEWD staff cited administrative capacity, bottleneck avoidance, demographic performance tracking, and NC Exclusive Emoluments Clause legal constraints as reasons to finalize a CDFI-administered loan model for July 1.
conflicts.resolution: Council suspended the rules 6-0 and voted unanimously 6-0 to allocate $1 million to the small business relief program while directing staff to finalize the framework.

conflicts.issue: Virtual-Only Community Engagement and Participatory Budgeting Cycle 2 Timing
conflicts.summary: Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned proceeding with Participatory Budgeting Cycle 2 in Fall 2020 under virtual-only engagement while deferring the Strategic Plan refresh to 2021.
conflicts.side_a_position: Virtual-only community engagement poses unresolved equity and public-health barriers that make launching Participatory Budgeting Cycle 2 in Fall 2020 problematic.

The same virtual-access objections used to hold up filling the Ward 3 Council vacancy apply to selecting artists or launching Participatory Budgeting solely online.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain the pre-existing 2021 schedule for the Strategic Plan refresh while proceeding with Fall 2020 Participatory Budgeting planning.
side_b_arguments: Staff noted the Strategic Plan refresh had always been scheduled for 2021 rather than being delayed specifically over virtual engagement.
conflicts.resolution: Informational discussion; no formal vote taken.

meetings.title: Special Virtual Durham City Council August 27, 2020 (w/ captions)
meetings.executive_summary: In this captioned broadcast of the August 27, 2020 special virtual meeting, all six seated members of the Durham City Council interviewed the five finalists for the Ward 3 City Council vacancy, beginning with opening remarks and questioning of Anita Daniels-Kenney on housing wealth grants, decriminalizing drug paraphernalia in favor of mental-health treatment, and Northeast Central Durham community engagement. Following the interviews, Council took up an emergency $338,000 request from the City's $5 million COVID Relief Fund to extend community learning centers—including downtown capacity at Kates Corner and six school-affiliated sites—for 338 students from six weeks to 11 weeks. Council voted unanimously 6-0 on a roll-call motion by Charlie Reece, seconded by Jillian Johnson, to suspend the rules, and then passed the $338,000 allocation 5-1 on a motion by Mark-Anthony Middleton, seconded by Jillian Johnson, with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting Nay over transparency, late agenda placement, and county school-funding obligations.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Simultaneous Spanish Interpretation, and Interview Rules
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the special meeting to interview the five Ward 3 vacancy finalists, working with Council Member Javiera Caballero, the City Clerk, and Spanish interpreter Muadado to configure Zoom's simultaneous Spanish interpretation channel. Mayor Schewel explained that each candidate would receive a three-minute opening statement, up to eight minutes of questions per council member in rotating alphabetical order, and five minutes from the Mayor.

agenda_items.title: Interviews of Ward 3 Vacancy Finalists (Including Anita Daniels-Kenney)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: First finalist Anita Daniels-Kenney shared her personal background in public housing and answered Javiera Caballero's questions on fiscal priorities following the city's $8.7 million fund balance draw (proposing grants to help three to five families purchase homes) and on reforming low-level drug paraphernalia charges by treating addiction as a mental illness. DeDreana Freeman then began questioning Daniels-Kenney on engaging previously unengaged residents, citing her Triangle United Way work in Northeast Central Durham, before the remaining interviews continued through the middle of the meeting.

agenda_items.title: COVID Relief Fund Request of $338,000 for Community Learning Centers
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Presenters Mr. Perry, Ms. Gonzalez Smith, and Mrs. Zagbaya requested $338,000 from the City's COVID Relief Fund to bridge Durham County's six-week commitment up to 11 weeks for 338 students across six schools and partner sites such as Kates Corner downtown (~80 seats), while noting $202,000 as a nine-week alternative figure and confirming DPS had not guaranteed transportation. Deputy City Attorney Don O'Toole noted he could not immediately answer legal scope questions in City Attorney Rehberg's absence, and council members criticized the nearly 55-45 city-county split, the lack of work-session agenda notice, and the need for Durham County and DPS to shoulder ongoing funding. After a 6-0 roll-call suspension of the rules, Council approved the $338,000 expenditure 5-1 with DeDreana Freeman dissenting.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 5-1 (Roll Call; preceded by 6-0 rule suspension)

votes.item_title: Motion to Suspend the Rules for Action on $338,000 Community Learning Centers Request
votes.discussion_detail: After Charlie Reece raised a point of order requiring a rule suspension to vote on the special-meeting item, Reece moved and Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson seconded suspending the rules. All six seated council members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Approve $338,000 Expenditure from COVID Relief Fund for Community Learning Centers
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson seconded approving $338,000 from the COVID Relief Fund for community learning centers. meetings.title: Special Virtual Durham City Council August 24, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting virtually on August 24, 2020 with all six seated members present, the Durham City Council convened to select finalists from 12 applicants for the Ward 3 council vacancy. On a 6-0 roll-call motion by Charlie Reece, seconded by DeDreana Freeman, Council voted to accept Micah Furlong's application as timely after Furlong registered to vote on August 21 upon learning of the registration gap. Following an electronic ballot tallied by the City Clerk, Council voted unanimously 6-0 on a motion by Charlie Reece, seconded by Javiera Caballero, to advance the five candidates who received at least four votes—Anita Daniels-Kenney, Leonardo Q. Williams, Pierce Freelon, Sheila Ann Huggins (five votes each), and Sarah Sinning (four votes). Council then resolved differences over interview length, PowerPoints, finalist count, and advance question sharing by agreeing to three-minute spoken opening statements, up to eight minutes of questioning per council member with optional advance question sharing, and rotating first questioners alphabetically on August 27.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Roll Call Following Zoom Outage
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel waited for colleagues experiencing nationwide Zoom login problems and thanked the Clerk's Office and Technology Solutions for resolving access. The City Clerk called the roll at 00:02:01, confirming all six seated members were present.

agenda_items.title: Consideration of Micah Furlong's Ward 3 Application
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel explained that all 12 applicants who submitted by 5:00 p.m. on August 20 passed county tax verification, but Micah Furlong was not yet registered to vote at the time of checking and went to the Board of Elections on August 21 to register. Charlie Reece recommended considering Furlong's application based on good-faith effort and prompt correction, and Council approved his motion 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Electronic Ballot and Selection of Five Ward 3 Finalists
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After DeDreana Freeman resolved an Outlook form permission issue and all six members submitted electronic ballots, the City Clerk reported four applicants received five votes and one received four votes. Council voted unanimously 6-0 to advance the five finalists—Anita Daniels-Kenney, Leonardo Q. Williams, Pierce Freelon, Sheila Ann Huggins, and Sarah Sinning.

agenda_items.title: August 27 Finalist Interview Structure, Time Limits, and Question Sharing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated whether to keep eight-minute questioning rounds or reduce them to five minutes, whether to permit PowerPoint slides or narrow the pool to four finalists, and whether to share questions beforehand. Council agreed to schedule 50-minute slots starting at 5:00 p.m. on August 27 with three-minute spoken opening statements (no PowerPoints), up to eight minutes per council member (five minutes for the Mayor last), alphabetical rotation of the lead questioner, and optional advance question sharing.

votes.item_title: Consider Ward 3 Applicant Micah Furlong's Application Alongside Other Applications
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded allowing Micah Furlong's application to be considered despite registering to vote on August 21 after the August 20 filing deadline. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain the established eight-minute questioning cap and preserve unscripted live questioning (or require PowerPoints if time is cut).
side_b_arguments: Council is a deliberative body that needs to see candidates think and engage on their feet rather than read scripted answers.
Individual members can already govern themselves and use fewer than eight minutes without lowering the formal cap.
Cutting questioning to five minutes without a PowerPoint option could limit the information gathered from candidates.
disagreements.resolution: Council maintained five finalists, kept the eight-minute cap (with Charlie Reece voluntarily taking five minutes), allowed optional advance sharing of questions and candidate materials, and prohibited PowerPoints in three-minute openings.

disagreements.issue: Gun Violence Response Priorities (ShotSpotter and Violence Interrupters) vs. Participatory Budgeting Equity Scrutiny
disagreements.summary: During a wide-ranging work session debate following recent fatal gun violence, council members clashed over prioritizing urgent gun-violence interventions such as ShotSpotter and violence interrupters versus repeated critiques of Participatory Budgeting's equity outcomes.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prioritize immediate action and funding for gun-violence interventions—including violence interrupters and testing ShotSpotter—while subjecting all city initiatives, including Participatory Budgeting, to equal equity scrutiny.

Council must schedule concrete funding and operational steps for violence interrupters and gun-violence prevention.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid conflating the gun-violence crisis with Participatory Budgeting criticism, correct incomplete PB demographic data claims, and schedule a dedicated PB staff and NCCU evaluation briefing alongside advancing the Community Safety Task Force and violence interrupters.
side_b_arguments: Claims that Participatory Budgeting failed its equity goals rely on incomplete demographic data because paper ballots and DPS student votes lacked racial data.
PB staff, the steering committee, and North Carolina Central University produced a full evaluation with improvement proposals that merit an accurate agenda briefing.
Crisis response and expanding violence interrupters should move forward in concert with the Community Safety & Wellness Task Force.
disagreements.resolution: Informational discussion; Mayor Steve Schewel agreed to work with the City Manager to schedule future work-session discussions on both gun-violence/violence-interrupter funding and the Participatory Budgeting evaluation.

meetings.title: Special Durham City Council Meeting May 27, 2020 (with closed captions)
meetings.executive_summary: In the closed-captioned broadcast of Durham City Council's May 27, 2020 Day 1 FY 2020-21 virtual budget work session, all six seated council members reviewed COVID-19 revenue losses and department updates covering pay and benefits, General Services, Parks and Recreation, and Transportation. Budget Director Bertha Johnson detailed holding the property tax rate flat, keeping the collection rate at 99.6% rather than 99% (a $1 million loss from February projections), projecting flat motor vehicle taxes, absorbing a 25% Powell Bill reduction, and drawing down fund balance at levels not seen since 2009. Council members questioned Transportation on bus sanitation, GoDurham mask penetration, 12-to-18-month parking operations, and slow streets; DeDreana Freeman urged stronger racial equity rigor in budget cuts, and Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and Charlie Reece flagged the new Transportation Financial Manager position for follow-up review. No formal votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Day 1 Budget Work Session Introduction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the 10:00 a.m. virtual budget work session and thanked budget, finance, technology, and clerk staff. City Manager Tom Bonfield introduced the two-day hybrid COVID-19 budget review, and Budget Director Bertha Johnson outlined Day 1 topics including revenue, pay and benefits, General Services, Parks and Recreation, and Transportation.

agenda_items.title: General Fund Revenue Projections, Property Tax Base, and Powell Bill Reduction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson reviewed FY 2020-21 General Fund revenue assumptions compared to February 14 pre-COVID estimates, noting no property tax rate increase, 2.31% assessed value growth led by real property, flat motor vehicle taxes, and holding the tax collection rate at 99.6% rather than raising it to 99%. She confirmed a newly incorporated 25% loss in state Powell Bill street-aid funding and substantial fund balance utilization, while reminding residents to separate city and county property tax bills.

agenda_items.title: Transit Mask Penetration, Bus Sanitation, Parking, Slow Streets, and Budget Equity
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members asked Transportation staff about GoDurham rider mask usage, bus sanitation protocols while offline, parking revenue recovery over the next 12 to 18 months, and slow-streets planning with cycling and pedestrian advocates. DeDreana Freeman warned against rushing cost-cutting decisions without deeper racial equity accountability, while staff emphasized that GoDurham investments represent the largest budget increase and disproportionately serve riders of color (about 90% of ridership).

agenda_items.title: Flagged Follow-Up Items: Transportation Financial Manager and Parks & Rec Staffing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel thanked Charlie Reece and Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson for sharing presiding duties, and City Manager Tom Bonfield stated all service restoration uses an equity lens. Jillian Johnson and Charlie Reece placed the proposed Transportation Financial Manager position on the follow-up list (noting the proposal to shift its funding from General Fund to Transit), while Javiera Caballero asked about CARES Act options, requested a breakdown of Parks and Recreation kept versus furloughed staff, and praised maintaining in-house custodial living wages before the meeting adjourned at 1:27 p.m.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session May 21, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting virtually on May 21, 2020, all six seated Durham City Council members passed nine unanimous 6-0 roll-call votes spanning priority agenda items, COVID-19 mask distribution, board Zoom security, and small-business relief. After DeDreana Freeman urged directing Cover Durham mask funds to local or people-of-color-owned businesses rather than Original Mattress Factory in Raleigh, Council unanimously amended and approved 6-0 the mask funding transfer to prioritize transit riders in distribution and prioritize hiring people of color. Following a Zoom-bombing incident at the Environmental Affairs Board meeting, Council accepted Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson's proposal to fund four shared Zoom webinar licenses rather than 20 individual licenses and passed it 6-0 alongside DeDreana Freeman's call for liaison training. At the close of the session, following sharp council criticism from Mark-Anthony Middleton, Jillian Johnson, and DeDreana Freeman over Office of Economic and Workforce Development (OEWD) delays and equity barriers in the proposed small-business loan program, Council suspended the rules and voted 6-0 to allocate $1 million for the small business relief program before settling the upcoming regular agenda 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the 1:00 p.m. virtual work session to order, and the clerk confirmed all six seated council members present. Mark-Anthony Middleton commended Durham Clergy United for announcing they would refrain from holding mass in-person religious gatherings despite a federal court ruling, and members discussed COVID-19's disproportionate toll on communities of color.

agenda_items.title: Forest Hills Neighborhood Protection Overlay and FY 2021 Stormwater Rate Proposal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield presented two priority items: revising Agenda Item 25 (initiating a Forest Hills Neighborhood Protection Overlay) from a public hearing to routine consent, and adding Agenda Item 27 (FY 2021 stormwater rate proposal) to schedule a June 1 public hearing. Council approved the manager's priority items 6-0 on roll call.

agenda_items.title: Cover Durham Phase 1 Mask Distribution Project Funding
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a 6-0 vote to consider the clerk's priority items, the City Clerk read details from coordinator Isaac Haran on Phase 1 of Cover Durham to distribute 50,000 reusable masks free to low-income and disproportionately Black neighborhoods via the Community Health Coalition, sourced from Original Mattress Factory in Raleigh. After DeDreana Freeman pushed to support local Durham or POC-owned producers such as LCI, Council suspended the rules 6-0 and passed Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson's motion (seconded by Mark-Anthony Middleton) 6-0 to approve the fund transfer with friendly amendments prioritizing transit riders in distribution and hiring people of color.

agenda_items.title: Zoom Webinar Licenses to Prevent Zoom-Bombing of Boards and Commissions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported a severe Zoom-bombing incident at the Environmental Affairs Board meeting the prior evening and proposed funding 20 Zoom webinar licenses ($40/month each, up to $5,800 from the $5,000 volunteer reception budget) to restrict public participant audio/video. Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson pointed out at most four board meetings ever overlap simultaneously so four shared licenses would suffice, and DeDreana Freeman stressed training tech liaisons on webinar controls; Council suspended the rules 6-0 and approved the expenditure 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Small Business COVID-19 Relief Loan Program Structure and $1 Million City Allocation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD presented proposed eligibility rules for a small business loan fund (independently owned local businesses operating 18+ months, priority for Neighborhood Revitalization and Opportunity Zones, fair-and-above credit scores, and Duke University's $1 million challenge) targeting a June council vote and July 1 check writing. Council members voiced strong dissatisfaction over the omitted budget amount, lack of a selected CDFI partner, slow July 1 timeline, and equity criteria; after suspending the rules 6-0, Council voted unanimously 6-0 to allocate $1 million to the small business relief program.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff summarized the settled agenda placing Items 1-11 and 13-17 on Consent and Items 12 and 25 on the General Business Agenda. Council approved the agenda 6-0 on roll call before adjourning at 5:10 p.m.

votes.discussion_detail: Council moved and seconded adding the City Clerk's two priority items to the work session discussion. The roll call passed unanimously 6-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Council moved and seconded suspending the rules to take immediate action on the Cover Durham mask transfer. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded approving the transfer of funds for Cover Durham masks, incorporating friendly amendments requesting the nonprofit prioritize transit riders in mask distribution and prioritize hiring people of color in distribution efforts. votes.discussion_detail: Following discussion of Zoom webinar controls and liaison training, Council moved and seconded suspending the rules for an immediate vote. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.discussion_detail: Council moved and seconded authorizing the City Clerk to spend necessary month-to-month funds (reallocated from the volunteer reception line item, pursuing four shared licenses to minimize cost) to provide Zoom webinar security for boards and commissions. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.discussion_detail: Council moved and seconded suspending the rules to vote immediately on allocating $1 million to the small business relief program. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.discussion_detail: Council moved and seconded formally allocating $1 million for Durham's upcoming small business COVID-19 relief program in response to Duke University's $1 million challenge and council concern over delayed disbursement. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

disagreements.summary: Council members sharply criticized OEWD's presentation for omitting a concrete fund size, delaying check writing until July 1 while searching for a CDFI partner, and relying on traditional underwriting criteria that could preserve racial disparities.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting May 4, 2020 (with closed captions)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the May 4, 2020 virtual Durham City Council meeting with all six seated members present (Ward 3 remained vacant). During announcements, council members commemorated 24 Durham COVID-19 fatalities and late Carolina Times publisher Kenneth Edmonds, urged Northgate Mall's owners to support displaced tenants and workers after the mall's closure, and highlighted community-led small business relief efforts for firms ineligible for federal PPP loans. The council unanimously approved the consent agenda 6-0—including an updated Item 18 depositing proceeds from the sale of 1415 West Club Boulevard into the Dedicated Housing Fund, the Housing for New Hope unsheltered coordinating agency contract, and a Police District 1 substation lease at 915 Holloway Street. Council then voted 6-0 to adopt guidelines crafted by Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and Council Member Javiera Caballero permitting optional, no-penalty virtual meetings via Zoom for city boards, committees, and commissions.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Moment of Silence, Pledge, Roll Call, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the virtual meeting to order, led a moment of silence honoring 24 Durham residents lost to COVID-19 and late Carolina Times publisher Kenneth Edmonds, and Council Member Charlie Reece led the Pledge of Allegiance before all six seated members answered roll call. Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton and Reece discussed the closing of Northgate Mall and urged its owners to assist displaced tenants and reassign workers, while Council Member DeDreana Freeman announced a local small business relief fund with NCCU School of Business, Communities in Partnership, and Resilient Ventures.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items and Consent Agenda (Items 1–4, 6–13, 17–20)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield reported that Item 18 (sale of 1415 West Club Boulevard to Garman Homes LLC) was updated per council direction so sale proceeds deposit into the Dedicated Housing Fund. Council Member Freeman noted appreciation for added workforce statistics before moving to approve the consent agenda, which also included board appointments, the Housing for New Hope unsheltered coordinating agency contract, water/utility contracts, the Police District 1 substation lease at 915 Holloway Street, the recyclable materials contract amendment, and the Durham County Transit Plan.

agenda_items.title: Guidelines for Virtual Operation of Boards, Committees, and Commissions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and Council Member Javiera Caballero presented guidelines allowing boards and commissions to meet optionally via Zoom (using publicly viewable webinar links compliant with open meetings law and newly signed Senate Bill 704), prohibiting in-person meetings, waiving attendance penalties, and designating a tech liaison per board. City Clerk Diana Schreiber reported that about 10 boards responded positively to a readiness poll, while City Attorney Kim Rehberg and Manager Bonfield addressed SB 704 streaming and quasi-judicial considerations for the Planning Commission and Board of Adjustment.

meetings.title: Special Virtual Durham City Council April 24, 2020  (with closed captions)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the April 24, 2020 special virtual budget work session with all six seated council members present. City Manager Tom Bonfield and Budget Director Bertha Johnson reported that COVID-19 revenue losses had widened the projected FY 2020-21 General Fund shortfall from $750,000 in February to between $11.8 million and $12.5 million due to lower tax collection assumptions and sharp drops in sales and occupancy taxes. Council gave informal consensus guidance (without formal votes) to hold General Fund (30.8 cents) and Dedicated Housing Fund (2.0 cents) tax rates flat, lower the General Fund balance floor from 16.7% to 12%, cap water/sewer increases at 3%, maintain street resurfacing at $6 million, reserve up to $5 million for COVID-19 needs, and permit review of employee pay increases and 401(k) contributions. Members also favored keeping the BID tax at 7 cents while redirecting DDI funds to small business relief and agreed to revisit the Dedicated Housing Fund separately before the May 18 budget presentation.

agenda_items.title: FY 2020-21 Revised Revenue Projections and Multi-Year Financial Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield and Budget Director Bertha Johnson (with Assistant Director John Allore) briefed council on COVID-19 fiscal impacts, showing the projected FY 2020-21 General Fund gap grew from $750,000 in February to roughly $11.8–$12.5 million. Revised assumptions cut property tax collection from 99.6% to 99%, held vehicle taxes flat, projected a 10% ($2.3 million) sales tax loss, and flagged a potential 30% occupancy tax drop (~$800,000 additional gap) reported by Discover Durham.

agenda_items.title: Revisions to FY 2020-21 Budget Development Guidelines (Revenues and Expenditures)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council walked through proposed guideline edits prioritizing COVID-19 needs and pausing new strategic initiatives ahead of the May 18 budget presentation. Consensus guidance supported keeping General Fund (30.8 cents) and Dedicated Housing Fund (2.0 cents) rates flat, lowering the fund balance floor from 16.7% to 12% and allowing fund balance to cover revenue losses, capping water/sewer increases at 3%, maintaining street resurfacing at $6 million and maintenance replacement at $1 million, setting aside up to $5 million for COVID-19 response, and allowing review of employee pay and 5% supplemental retirement adjustments.

agenda_items.title: Enterprise Funds and Downtown Business Improvement District (BID) Tax Rate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget staff reviewed Transit ($12.2 million regional CARES Act split pending May 8 MPO vote; no fund balance amid fare suspension and 16-passenger limits), Solid Waste ($6 million fund balance), and Parking ($8.3 million fund balance). Regarding the BID tax rate scenarios (7.0, 6.0, 5.73, and 5.0 cents), Council Members Middleton, Johnson, Caballero, and Freeman expressed support for maintaining 7 cents while cutting the General Fund transfer and redirecting DDI funds toward downtown small business relief and staff retention.

agenda_items.title: Dedicated Housing Fund, Small Business Assistance, and Stay-at-Home Order Extension
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Manager Bonfield noted Fallon police-headquarters sale proceeds were budgeted in the General Fund rather than the Dedicated Housing Fund, and council agreed to hold a separate housing budget discussion later. Council discussed pairing city efforts with Duke University's $1 million small business fund to reach undocumented and disadvantaged businesses, and Mayor Schewel announced an amended Stay-at-Home Order extending to May 15 with curbside retail pickup and real estate adjustments.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session April 23, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the April 23, 2020 virtual work session with all six seated members present. Council voted unanimously 6-0 to add City Clerk Diana Schreiber's priority item on reactivating boards and commissions virtually and later tasked Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and Council Member Javiera Caballero with drafting optional, no-penalty virtual meeting guidelines. Members pulled and reviewed consent items ahead of the May 4 meeting—including the Housing for New Hope unsheltered coordinating agency contract, the Police District 1 substation lease (where DeDreana Freeman urged Office of Equity and Inclusion review), the 1415 West Club Boulevard sale (which Johnson proposed directing to the Dedicated Housing Fund), the recycling contract cost swing, and the Durham County Transit Plan amid GoDurham's 16-rider bus cap. After resolving ballot ties for board and commission nominations, council voted unanimously 6-0 to settle the May 4 agenda.

agenda_items.title: Clerk Priority Item Addition and Administrative Consent Agenda Pulls
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 6-0 to add City Clerk Diana Schreiber's priority item on reactivating boards and commissions to the end of the work session. Mayor Schewel noted minor corrections to the March 5 minutes and members pulled Items 10, 17, 18, 19, and 20 for discussion ahead of the May 4 regular meeting.

agenda_items.title: Item 10: Contract with Housing for New Hope as Unsheltered Coordinating Agency
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff (Karen Lado and Hanaleah Hoberman) answered questions from Mayor Schewel and Mayor Pro Tem Johnson regarding COVID-19 training for street outreach workers, medical partnerships with Duke Clinic and Lincoln Community Health, moving medically vulnerable unsheltered residents into hotels, and Housing for New Hope's expansion to five dedicated program staff.

agenda_items.title: Items 17 & 18: Police District 1 Substation Lease and 1415 W. Club Blvd. Property Sale
agenda_items.discussion_summary: On Item 17 (10-year, $2.9 million Police District 1 substation lease at 915 Holloway St.), Council Member Freeman questioned General Services staff (David Fleischer) on the absence of Office of Equity and Inclusion review for city leases. On Item 18 (sale of a 30x36-foot residual parcel at 1415 W. Club Blvd.), Freeman asked about affordability conditions while Mayor Pro Tem Johnson proposed directing proceeds into the Dedicated Housing Fund and creating a standing policy for future residential land sales.

agenda_items.title: Items 19 & 20: Recycling Processing Contract and Durham County Transit Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Solid Waste staff reported recycling costs swung from $450,000 revenue to over $100/ton (versus ~$40/ton landfilling), while continuing single-stream collection with public education and regional Triangle J coordination. Transportation Director Sean Egan and MPO representative Aaron Cain reviewed the $670,000 Durham County Transit Plan consultant contract and addressed questions from Mayor Schewel and Council Member Freeman about GoDurham's 16-passenger social-distancing cap leaving riders at stops and plans to deploy follow-on buses.

agenda_items.title: Virtual Operations Guidelines for Boards, Committees, and Commissions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated how to allow eager advisory boards to resume work virtually without disadvantaging members lacking internet access, childcare bandwidth, or time during the pandemic, with Reece and Freeman urging caution and Middleton supporting authorizing but not mandating meetings. Council tasked Mayor Pro Tem Johnson and Council Member Caballero with drafting voluntary, no-penalty guidelines using Zoom or Microsoft Teams with tech liaisons and telephone dial-in options.

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Nominations and Settling May 4 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Because six seated members required four votes for nomination, council broke ties via announced vote switches for the Citizens Advisory Committee (Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman), BPAC (Shyla Nappe and Jasmine Joyner), Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee (Cesar Angiano-Ortiz and Shan Almonte), and Recreation Advisory Commission (Cedric Burke), and confirmed Appearance, DPAC Oversight, and Workers Rights nominees. City Manager Bonfield then recommended placing Items 1–4, 6–13, and 17–20 on the May 4 consent agenda, which council approved 6-0.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council April 20, 2020 (with closed captions)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the April 20, 2020 virtual City Council meeting with all six seated members present following Vernetta Alston's resignation. Council announced an expansion of written public comments from 250 to 4,000 characters, approved the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 8) 6-0, and approved Item 8 (Emergency Response Plan and Source Water Risk and Resilience Plan) 6-0. Turning to the Ward 3 vacancy after community groups criticized the April 6 appointment timeline during the pandemic, council accepted legal guidance from City Attorney Kim Rehberg and voted unanimously 6-0 to rescind the April 6 timeline and unanimously 6-0 to proceed instead under N.C.G.S. § 160A-63 (via § 160A-3), removing the charter's 60-day special-election clock and targeting an August 6 check-in.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, COVID-19 Update, and Public Comment Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order with a moment of silence for 86 COVID-19 residents at a Durham rehabilitation facility and community deaths, followed by the Pledge and roll call. Schewel noted public comments on North Durham motorbikes and rent hardship, confirmed the public comment limit increased to 4,000 characters, and reviewed Duke health modeling showing slower case growth.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1–3, 5–7, 9–23, Excluding Item 8)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved all consent items except pulled Item 8, encompassing CDBG contracts with Urban Ministries and DHA for Laurel Oaks Townhomes, DHA's McDougall Terrace grant request, Eno River water-supply reclassification support, sewer manhole rehabilitation contracts, the Museum of Durham History lease, Hoover Road Park CMAR amendment, 2019 Q4 crime report, and the Ashton Place Development Loan commitment.

agenda_items.title: Item 8: Emergency Response Plan and Source Water Risk and Resilience Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman stated she pulled Item 8 to highlight appreciation for staff's quick response, after which council passed the item unanimously by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Rescission of April 6 Ward 3 Timeline and Election to Proceed Under N.C.G.S. § 160A-63
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton urged rescinding the April 6 appointment schedule due to pandemic access barriers raised by the Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People, People's Alliance, and Friends of Durham. After Council Member Charlie Reece and City Attorney Kim Rehberg outlined how N.C.G.S. § 160A-3 and § 160A-63 eliminate the charter's 60-day deadline while preserving appointment authority, council agreed to revisit the process on August 6 and passed both the rescission (6-0) and § 160A-63 election (6-0).
